p.src: After returning from the land of the kappa, for a while I could hardly bear the smell of human skin. Compared with us human beings, kappa are extraordinarily clean creatures. What is more, after seeing nothing but kappa, I found human heads positively uncanny. Perhaps you may not understand this. But eyes and mouths aside, the thing we call a nose somehow inspires a peculiar horror. Naturally, I contrived as far as possible to avoid meeting anyone. Yet I seem gradually to have grown accustomed to human beings again, and within about six months I began going everywhere as before. Even then, however, one troublesome thing remained: while talking, I would carelessly let a word from the language of the kappa country slip out. “Will you be at home tomorrow?” “Qua.” “What did you say?” “Oh, I mean that I will.” That was more or less how it would go. But about a year after I returned from the land of the kappa, a certain enterprise of mine ended in failure, and I… (When he reached this point, Dr. S warned him, “You had better not tell that story.” According to the doctor, whenever he tells this story, he becomes so violent that even the attendants cannot manage him.) Then let us leave that story alone. But because that enterprise had failed, I began longing to return once more to the land of the kappa. Yes. I did not want to “go” there. I began wanting to “go home” there. For by then, the land of the kappa felt like home to me. I quietly slipped out of the house and tried to board a train on the Chūō Line. Unfortunately, a policeman caught me on the way, and in the end I was put into this hospital. Even when I had first entered this hospital, I continued thinking about the land of the kappa.

I quietly slipped out of the house and tried to board a train on the Chūō Line.

Even when I had first entered this hospital, I continued thinking about the land of the kappa.

p.src: I wondered how Chack, the doctor, was getting on. Perhaps Magg, the philosopher, was still pondering something beneath his lantern of seven-colored glass. And above all, there was Lapp, the student with the rotting beak who had been my dearest friend—It was a cloudy afternoon, much like today. Lost in these memories, I was on the verge of crying out without thinking. For, though I had no idea when he had entered, a fisherman kappa named Bagg stood before me, bowing his head again and again. After I had regained my composure—I cannot even remember whether I wept or laughed. But of one thing I am certain: I was deeply moved to be speaking the language of the kappa country again after so long.

p.src: “Hey, Bag, what brings you here?” “Well, sir, I came to see how you were doing. I heard that you were ill.” “How did you learn of that?” “I heard it on the radio news.” Bag smiled with evident pride. “Even so, I’m surprised you managed to get here.” “Oh, it was no trouble at all. For a kappa, Tokyo’s rivers and canals are as good as streets.” It struck me anew that kappas, like frogs, were amphibious creatures. “But there aren’t any rivers around here.” “No, sir. To get up here, I came through the iron water mains. Then I simply opened a fire hydrant…” “You opened a fire hydrant?” “Have you forgotten, sir? There are mechanics among the kappas too.” After that, I received visits from various kappas every two or three days. According to Dr. S, my illness is dementia praecox. But Chack, that doctor, said—though this must surely be highly discourteous to you as well— that I was not the one suffering from dementia praecox; the real patients were Dr. S and all of you yourselves. Since even Chack the doctor comes to see me, it goes without saying that Lap the student and Magg the philosopher have visited too. Yet apart from Bag the fisherman, none of them ever calls during the day. They come two or three together only at night—and always on moonlit nights. Only last night, in the moonlight, I spoke with Gael, the president of the glass company, and Magg the philosopher. What is more, I had Kraback the musician play me a piece on the violin. Look, you can see that bouquet of black lilies on the desk over there, can’t you? Kraback brought that for me as a gift last night too.

p.src: But I am not as pessimistic as this poet. Not so long as the kappas keep coming to visit me from time to time—ah, I had forgotten something. You remember Pepp, the judge who was a friend of mine, don’t you? After losing his position, that kappa truly went mad. I hear he is now in an asylum in the land of the kappas. If only Dr. S would consent, I should like to go and visit him… (February 11, 1927)
